lessons.title: Growth Stages and Targets
lessons.body: From week 5 to market, your turkeys go through three clear stages: grower (5â12 weeks), developer (13â18 weeks), and finisher (19â24 weeks or more, depending on breed). Each stage has target weights and feed needs. For a broad-breasted white, aim for 5â7 kg live weight at 12 weeks, 9â12 kg at 18 weeks, and 14â18 kg at 24 weeks. Local or crossbreed turkeys grow slower: expect 3â4 kg at 12 weeks and 6â8 kg at 24 weeks. Weigh 10 birds every two weeks using a hanging scale or a bathroom scale (weigh yourself, then hold the bird). Record weights in a notebook. If average weight is more than 10% below target, check feed quality, space, and disease. At 8 weeks, separate males and females if you canâmales grow faster and need more feed. In hot African climates, turkeys eat less during midday; provide most feed early morning and late afternoon. By 16 weeks, start evaluating which birds to keep for breeding or sell as heavy roasters. Cull slow-growing, lame, or sick birds early to save feed. A turkey that reaches 2 kg at 8 weeks but only 4 kg at 16 weeks is not profitableâsell it as a small bird or use it for home consumption. Keep a simple chart on the wall: date, age, average weight, feed consumed. That chart tells you if you are on track.

lessons.title: Space Allowances
lessons.body: Turkeys need more space than chickens. Overcrowding causes feather pecking, cannibalism, poor growth, and disease. For grow-out pens, give 0.5 square meters per bird from 5 to 12 weeks, 1.0 square meter from 13 to 18 weeks, and 1.5 square meters from 19 weeks to market. If you keep turkeys on deep litter, use dry wood shavings, rice husks, or chopped maize cobsânever wet or mouldy litter. In free-range systems, allow 10â15 square meters per bird so they can graze. But even free-range birds need a sheltered house at night: 0.3â0.5 square meters per bird inside. Ventilation is critical. In hot climates, build open-sided houses with wire mesh walls and a solid roof. Air must move freely but not blow directly on the birds. If you smell ammonia, you need more ventilation or fresh litter. Feeders: allow 10 cm of linear feeder space per bird; drinkers: 2 cm per bird. For 50 birds at 16 weeks, you need about 50 square meters of floor space, 5 meters of feeder, and 1 meter of drinker. Use local materials: bamboo, mud bricks, thatch, or corrugated iron. Raise the house floor 15â20 cm above ground to prevent flooding. Add perchesâturkeys like to roost. Provide 20 cm of perch length per bird, 60 cm above the floor. Clean and disinfect the house between batches. If you see birds panting and holding wings away from the body, they are too hotâincrease shade and airflow immediately.

lessons.title: Feeding for Optimal Growth
lessons.body: Turkeys need high-protein feed for fast growth. From 5 to 8 weeks, feed a grower mash with 24â26% crude protein. From 9 to 16 weeks, use 20â22% protein. From 17 weeks to market, use 16â18% protein finisher feed. You can mix your own using locally available ingredients: maize (energy), soybean meal or groundnut cake (protein), fish meal (protein and minerals), and limestone or oyster shell (calcium). A simple 100 kg grower mix: 50 kg maize, 30 kg soybean meal, 10 kg fish meal, 5 kg wheat bran, 3 kg limestone, 1 kg salt, 1 kg vitamin-mineral premix. For finisher, reduce soybean to 20 kg and increase maize to 60 kg. Always mix well. Feed twice a dayâearly morning and late afternoon. Give only what birds can finish in 20 minutes to avoid waste and spoilage. A turkey eats about 0.5 kg feed per day at 8 weeks, 1 kg at 16 weeks, and 1.5 kg at 24 weeks. Provide clean water at all times; a turkey drinks 2â3 times its feed weight in water. In hot weather, add electrolytes (1 teaspoon salt + 1 teaspoon baking soda per 5 litres) once a week. Never feed mouldy maizeâit causes aflatoxin poisoning, which stunts growth and kills. Store feed in dry, raised containers. If you cannot afford commercial premix, use crushed termite mound soil or wood ash as a mineral source, but commercial premix is safer. Weigh feed weekly to track consumptionâif feed intake drops, check for disease or heat stress.

lessons.title: Health Monitoring
lessons.body: Walk through your turkeys at least twice a day. Look for signs of illness: drooping wings, ruffled feathers, closed eyes, greenish diarrhoea, coughing, sneezing, or sudden deaths. Isolate any sick bird immediately in a separate pen with clean water and feed. Common turkey diseases in Africa include Newcastle disease, fowl pox, coccidiosis, and blackhead. Vaccinate against Newcastle at 7 days (if not done earlier) and repeat every 3 months. For fowl pox, vaccinate at 8 weeks. Coccidiosis is controlled with amprolium in drinking water for 5 days, but prevention is better: keep litter dry and avoid overcrowding. Blackhead is a parasite that affects turkeys more than chickensâdo not keep turkeys with chickens, especially where chickens have access to soil. Deworm every 8 weeks with levamisole or albendazole. External parasites (lice, mites) are treated with dusting powder or ash. Keep a health record: date, symptoms, treatment, outcome. If more than 2 birds die in a week, call a vet or extension officer. In many African countries, government veterinary services are free or cheap. Also watch for injuries: turkeys can break legs if handled roughly. Provide soft bedding. If a bird has a wound, clean with warm salty water and apply iodine. Always wash your hands and boots before entering the penâyou can carry disease from other farms. Quarantine new birds for 3 weeks before mixing with your flock.

lessons.title: Handling and Moving Turkeys
lessons.body: Turkeys are strong and can injure themselves or you if handled wrongly. Never lift a turkey by its wings, legs, or neck. The correct method: approach calmly from the side, place one hand under the breast and the other hand over the back, holding the wings against the body. Lift smoothly and hold the bird close to your body for support. For large toms (over 10 kg), use a catching hook or a cloth sling. Move birds in the cool of the dayâearly morning or evening. Avoid chasing; it causes stress and heat exhaustion. Use a catching pen or a corner of the house with a temporary fence made of bamboo or netting. To move turkeys from one pen to another, herd them slowly with a wooden board or a stick, not by shouting. If you must transport them, use crates with ventilation holes. Give each bird 0.1 square meters of crate space. Do not stack crates more than three high. Cover the crate with a light cloth to reduce stress, but ensure airflow. Transport in a vehicle with open sides. For short distances, carry birds in baskets lined with soft grass. After moving, give water with vitamins for 2 days. Handle birds only when necessaryâevery handling event slows growth. Train your helpers on correct handling. If a bird struggles, put it down gently, let it calm, then try again. Never lift more than one bird at a time. For weighing, use a hanging scale with a cloth sling; it is quick and safe.

lessons.title: Pre-Market Preparation
lessons.body: Two weeks before selling, start preparing your turkeys for market. First, decide your market: live birds, dressed (slaughtered and plucked), or cut pieces. Live birds are easiestâyou need no special equipment. Dressed birds fetch higher prices but require a clean slaughter area, sharp knives, hot water (60â65Â°C) for plucking, and cold storage or immediate sale. If selling live, stop feeding 12 hours before transport to reduce defecation, but always provide water. Weigh each bird and sort into weight classes: small (under 5 kg), medium (5â8 kg), large (8â12 kg), extra-large (over 12 kg). Buyers pay more for uniform sizes. Clean the birdsâ feet and vent area with a damp cloth. For dressed birds, starve 8 hours, then slaughter by severing the jugular vein. Bleed fully, then scald and pluck. Remove head and feet. Chill in clean water with ice or in a refrigerator. If you have no cold storage, sell immediately. Package in clean plastic bags or wrap in banana leaves. Label with weight and date. Transport in clean crates or baskets. For live birds, tie legs loosely with soft ropeânever wire. Market early in the morning when it is cool. Take a few birds to show buyers before the main batch. Set a price based on local market rates: check prices at nearby markets or ask other farmers. Do not underpriceâturkey meat is premium. Keep records of sales and expenses to know your profit. After selling, clean and disinfect all crates and the slaughter area.

quiz.q: What is the target live weight for a broad-breasted white turkey at 12 weeks?
quiz.explanation: Broad-breasted whites should reach 5â7 kg at 12 weeks.

quiz.q: How often should you weigh a sample of turkeys during grow-out?
quiz.explanation: Weighing every two weeks helps track growth and catch problems early.

quiz.q: What should you do if average weight is more than 10% below target?
options: C) Check feed quality, space, and disease
D) Ignore it, turkeys grow at different rates
quiz.explanation: Below-target weight indicates a problem with feed, space, or health.

quiz.q: Why separate male and female turkeys at 8 weeks?
options: B) Males grow faster and need different feed
quiz.explanation: Males grow faster and have higher feed requirements, so separation allows targeted feeding.

quiz.q: When is the best time to provide most feed in hot African climates?
options: B) Early morning and late afternoon
quiz.explanation: Turkeys eat less during midday heat, so feed when it is cooler.

quiz.q: What is the recommended floor space per bird from 5 to 12 weeks?
quiz.explanation: Grower turkeys need 0.5 square meters per bird to prevent overcrowding.

quiz.q: What is a sign that your turkey house needs more ventilation?
quiz.explanation: Ammonia smell indicates poor air quality and need for more ventilation or fresh litter.

quiz.q: How much linear feeder space should each turkey have?
quiz.explanation: Allow 10 cm of feeder space per bird to ensure all can eat.

quiz.q: What is the ideal litter material for turkeys?
quiz.explanation: Dry wood shavings absorb moisture and reduce disease.

quiz.q: How high should perches be for turkeys?
quiz.explanation: Perches 60 cm above the floor suit turkeys' natural roosting behaviour.

quiz.q: What crude protein level is needed in grower feed from 5 to 8 weeks?
quiz.explanation: Young growers need 24â26% protein for rapid muscle and bone growth.

quiz.q: In a 100 kg grower mix, how much soybean meal is recommended?
quiz.explanation: 30 kg soybean meal provides the main protein source in this mix.

quiz.q: How much feed does a turkey eat per day at 16 weeks?
quiz.explanation: At 16 weeks, a turkey consumes about 1 kg of feed daily.

quiz.q: What is a sign of aflatoxin poisoning in turkeys?
quiz.explanation: Aflatoxin from mouldy feed stunts growth and can cause death.

quiz.q: How often should you provide electrolytes in hot weather?
quiz.explanation: Weekly electrolytes help replace salts lost through panting in heat.

quiz.q: Which disease should you vaccinate against at 8 weeks?
quiz.explanation: Fowl pox vaccination is recommended at 8 weeks.

quiz.q: Why should turkeys not be kept with chickens?
quiz.explanation: Chickens can carry Histomonas meleagridis, which causes blackhead in turkeys.

quiz.q: How often should you deworm turkeys?
quiz.explanation: Regular deworming every 8 weeks prevents internal parasite build-up.

quiz.q: What should you do if more than 2 birds die in a week?
options: C) Call a vet or extension officer
quiz.explanation: Multiple deaths indicate a serious problem requiring professional advice.

quiz.q: How should you lift a large turkey?
quiz.explanation: Supporting the breast and back prevents injury to the bird.

quiz.q: When is the best time to move turkeys?
quiz.explanation: Cooler times reduce stress and heat exhaustion during handling.

quiz.q: How much crate space per bird for transport?
quiz.explanation: 0.1 square meters per bird in crates allows adequate ventilation and movement.

quiz.q: What should you give turkeys after moving them?
quiz.explanation: Vitamin water helps birds recover from transport stress.

quiz.q: How long before transport should you stop feeding live birds?
quiz.explanation: 12 hours without feed reduces defecation during transport but water is still given.

quiz.q: What is the correct water temperature for scalding a turkey?
quiz.explanation: 60â65Â°C water loosens feathers without cooking the skin.

quiz.q: How should you sort turkeys for market?
quiz.explanation: Uniform weight classes attract better prices from buyers.

quiz.q: What is a good way to package dressed turkeys without refrigeration?
quiz.explanation: Banana leaves are clean, local, and help keep meat cool for short periods.

quiz.q: How should you tie live turkeys for market?
quiz.explanation: Soft rope tied loosely prevents injury and stress.

quiz.q: Why keep records of sales and expenses?
quiz.explanation: Records help you calculate profit and make better decisions next cycle.

quiz.q: What should you do after selling all birds?
options: B) Clean and disinfect crates and area
quiz.explanation: Cleaning and disinfecting prevents disease carry-over to the next batch.
